# Sum and product and dummy variable {#sec-sum}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
Acronyms in mathematics!
:::

People at the ministry in conservation are found of acronyms, PAEP etc. While they are fluent with that, they often do not realize that outsiders have no idea of what they are talking about. Conversely, when mathematicians are using acronyms (symbols) to condense a expression, it is universally unaccessible.

But there is a common denominator: acronyms and notations are incredible useful as long as one is fluent in them. And to parapharase Catie in Mean Girls : mathematics has the advantage that the notations are for the whole world. Multiplication is a notation used so not repeat addition $2 + 2 + 2 = 3 \times 2$ or a factorial $n! = 1 \times 2 \times 3 \times ... (n - 1) \times n$. Some notations are more notorious than other, which depends on frequency of usage.

Two fundamentally useful and notorious notation are the summation notation ($\sum$) and the product $\prod$. These also scare many people. Maybe because it starts with greek letter and also because it is often followed by more expressions.

With a bit of fluency in greek letter (@sec-greek), one observation is that $\sum$ is the greek of equivalent of capital S (short of sum), and $\pi$ is the equivalent of capital P (short for product). They are used when there is a repeating patterns in the expression that one wants to add or multiply.


## Formal {.unnumbered}
Here is one general form of a summation:

$$
\sum_{i = n_0}^{n_f} a_i = a_{n_0} + a_{n_0 + 1} + \cdots + a_{n_f - 1} + a_{n_f}
$$

<!-- or
$$
\sum_{i = n_0}^{n_f} a(i) = a(n_0) + a(n_0 + 1) + \cdots + a(n_f - 1) + a(n_f)
$$ -->

The strategy is to break down, identify, and interpret  each term^[always a good idea when looking at math notation].

- $\sum$ is symbol for summation
- $i$ is found under the summation $i = n_0$ and in the expression $a_i$ and is called the index of summation
- $n_0$ represent the first expression in the summation. i.e, replace $i$ in $a_i$ by $a_{n_0}$
- $n_f$ is the last expression which ends the summation

For the product, replace $+$ by $\times$
$$
\prod_{i = n_0}^{n_f} a_i = a_{n_0} \times a_{n_0 + 1} \times \cdots \times a_n
$$

In other words,  calculate the $a_i$ for each value in the discrete sequence of whole number $[n_0, \ldots, n_f ]$, the add with $\sum$ or multiply with $\pi$.

$i$ is called a dummy variable because the choice of the letter or notation does not affect the results.

## Examples {.unnumbered}

#### Understanding the dummy variable {.unnumbered}
- Identifying the role of the dummy variable
  $$
    \sum_{i = n_0}^{n_f} i^a = {n_0}^a + \cdots + {n_f}^a
  $$
- Using a different letter ($j$) to denote the dummy variable
  $$
    \sum_{j = n_0}^{n_f} j^a = {n_0}^a + \cdots + {n_f}^a
  $$

- Writing the dummy variable as an argument of a function instead of index
  $$
    \sum_{i = n_0}^{n_f} f(i) = f(n_0) + \cdots + f(n_f)
  $$

#### Concrete example OF summation {.unnumbered}
- A simple addition
  $$
    \sum_{i=0}^7 i = 0 + 1 + 2 + \cdots + 6 + 7
  $$
- Changing the range of i from 3 to 7
  $$
    \sum_{i=3}^7 i^2 =  3^2 + 4^2 + \cdots + 6^2 + 7^2
  $${#eq-sum37}

- Not getting distracted by the expression after the summation
  $$
    \sum_{i=0}^7 \sin(\frac{1}{i+1}) = \sin(\frac{1}{1+ 0}) + \sin(\frac{1}{ 1+ 1}) + \cdots + \sin(\frac{1}{7+1})
  $$

Same example but replacing $\sum$ with $\prod$.


- The factorial is used so often that it was given its own and compact notation
  $$
    \prod_{i = 1}^n i = 1 \times 2 \times 3 \times \cdots \times (n-1) \times n = n!
  $$

- Same as above (@eq-sum37) but with product
  $$
    \prod_{i=3}^7 i^2 = 3^2 \times 4^2 \times  \cdots \times 6^2 \times 7^2
  $$

- The summation can be infinite
  $$
    \sum_{i = 0}^\infty \frac{1}{i!} = \frac{1}{0!} + \frac{1}{1!} +\frac{1}{2!} + \cdots = 2.71\ldots = e
  $$


## Tips and warning {.unnumbered}
- Whenever facing a complicated expression, break it down piece by piece. The most important is to understand how the expression after the symbol $\sum$ changes as the dummy variable changes.
- Sometimes it helps to take a pen and paper and try with the first few terms
- The dummy by a single letter $i$, $j$, or $k$. Why more than minimal.
- To complicate a bit, instead of a increment of 1, the set of value the dummy variable takes can also be defined by a set, in that case the set should be defined explicitly. $\Omega = [2, 9, 21, 25]$, then
  $$
    \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} a_\omega = a_2 + a_9 + a_{21} + a_{25}
  $$

### Semantic/Notation/Terminology {.unnumbered}

- The summation index $i$ is also called dummy variable or iterator in computer science and programming
- The range of values be below and above or next to the symbol
  $$
    \sum_{i = 1}^4 \text{ or } \sum\nolimits_{i = 1}^4
  $$
